title: {{NAME}} and the Dinosaur Who Made a Friend
moral: Even the biggest, scariest-looking creatures just want someone to play with.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a khaki explorer shirt, brown cargo shorts, and sturdy tan boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} had read every dinosaur book in the library, but nothing prepared him for the morning he found giant three-toed footprints leading from the river into the forest behind his house.

Each print was as wide as a dinner table. Fresh mud was still oozing back into the edges.

"A real one," he breathed. Then he did the bravest thing he could think of: he followed them.

pages.content:
He found it in a clearing: a young Brachiosaurus, not much bigger than a school bus, with enormous brown eyes and a neck that bent in a graceful curve to sniff at a patch of ferns.

Beside it, a family of rabbits sat completely unbothered.

The dinosaur looked at {{NAME}} and sneezed, scattering fern fronds everywhere. The rabbits hopped one step sideways, then went back to eating.

"You're not scary at all," {{NAME}} said, surprised.

pages.content:
The Brachiosaurus wanted to play, but had no idea how.

It tried nudging {{NAME}} with its nose. Too hard: he flew sideways into a fern bush.

It tried lying down. A tree fell over.

"Okay," said {{NAME}}, picking leaf bits from his hair. "Let me teach you. Watch the rabbits. They chase each other. Ready?"

He ran. The Brachiosaurus thundered after him, shaking the earth with every step, honking with joy, while rabbits scattered in all directions.

pages.content:
By afternoon, they had invented a game: {{NAME}} would hide behind a tree, and the Brachiosaurus would use its long neck to find him by sniffing, like a very large, very slow game of hide and seek.

The animals gathered to watch. Squirrels perched on the Brachiosaurus's back. A fox sat on a log judging proceedings with great seriousness.

"You've never lost," {{NAME}} told the dinosaur. "Not once."

pages.content:
When the sun turned orange and the fireflies began their first slow blinks, the Brachiosaurus lay down in the clearing with a long, satisfied sigh.

The rabbits nestled against its side. The squirrels tucked in near its neck. The fox curled by its tail.

{{NAME}} leaned against its warm flank and looked up at the first star.

"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.

The Brachiosaurus made a deep, gentle rumble that rolled through the ground and up through his back and felt exactly like yes.
